osces.title: Acute Severe Asthma Exacerbation - Emergency Management and Severity Assessment

patient_scenario.chief_complaint: Severe shortness of breath for 6 hours, unable to complete sentences, using reliever inhaler every 20 minutes without relief
patient_scenario.history_presenting_illness: 28-year-old woman with known asthma presenting with acute severe exacerbation. Symptoms began this morning after exposure to classroom dust during cleaning. Progressive worsening despite using salbutamol inhaler 2 puffs every 20 minutes for the past 6 hours (total >30 puffs). Now unable to speak in full sentences, feeling exhausted. No chest pain or fever. Has had 2 previous hospital admissions for asthma, last one 18 months ago requiring 3 days admission. No previous ICU admissions. Triggered by dust, pollen, and viral infections. Usually well-controlled on preventer therapy.
patient_scenario.allergies: Penicillin (rash as child - unconfirmed), dust mite allergy confirmed on skin prick testing

social_history.exercise: Regular yoga 3 times per week when well, currently unable to exercise due to symptoms
social_history.occupation_detail: Primary school teacher, Year 2 classroom. Exposed to dust, chalk, classroom pets. School currently undergoing renovations with increased dust exposure

patient_scenario.family_history: Mother has asthma, father has allergic rhinitis, younger brother has eczema (strong atopic family history)

examination_findings.respiratory: General inspection: Patient sitting upright, unable to complete sentences (speaking 3-4 words per breath), using accessory muscles of respiration (sternocleidomastoid, scalenes prominent), pursed lip breathing. Increased work of breathing evident. Inspection: Symmetrical chest expansion but reduced. No cyanosis. Intercostal recession present. Palpation: Reduced chest expansion bilaterally, tactile vocal fremitus difficult to assess due to poor air entry. Percussion: Hyperresonant throughout both lung fields. Auscultation: Bilateral widespread expiratory polyphonic wheeze audible without stethoscope, prolonged expiratory phase, reduced air entry throughout all zones bilaterally. No focal crackles. Silent chest not present (still audible wheeze indicates some air movement). Peak expiratory flow rate (PEFR) 180 L/min (predicted 450 L/min = 40% predicted, indicating severe exacerbation)
examination_findings.cardiovascular: Heart sounds dual, tachycardic but regular rhythm. No murmurs appreciated (difficult to assess over wheeze). JVP not elevated. Peripheral pulses present and equal. Capillary refill <2 seconds. No peripheral oedema
examination_findings.other_systems: Abdomen soft and non-tender, no organomegaly. Neurological: Alert but distressed, GCS 15/15, able to follow commands. No focal neurology

investigations.chest_xray: Hyperinflated lung fields bilaterally with flattened hemidiaphragms. No focal consolidation. No pneumothorax. No pneumomediastinum. Cardiac silhouette normal size. Clear costophrenic angles. Interpretation: Changes consistent with acute asthma exacerbation, no complications identified
investigations.spirometry: Unable to perform reliably due to acute severe symptoms. Previous spirometry 6 months ago (when well): FEV1 3.2L (92% predicted), FVC 4.1L (95% predicted), FEV1/FVC ratio 78%. Post-bronchodilator FEV1 increased to 3.6L (13% improvement, confirming reversible airways obstruction)
investigations.blood_gas: Arterial blood gas on room air: pH 7.44, PaCO2 35 mmHg, PaO2 62 mmHg, HCO3 24 mmol/L, Base excess 0, Lactate 1.8 mmol/L. Interpretation: Type 1 respiratory failure (hypoxaemia without hypercapnia). Normal pH and PaCO2 in context of severe asthma is concerning - indicates patient tiring, as typically would expect respiratory alkalosis (low PaCO2) due to hyperventilation. Rising or normal PaCO2 in acute asthma indicates impending respiratory failure and potential need for ICU
investigations.bloods: Full blood count: Hb 138 g/L, WCC 11.2 × 10⁹/L (neutrophils 8.1, lymphocytes 2.4, eosinophils 0.5), Platelets 245 × 10⁹/L. Electrolytes: Na 138 mmol/L, K 3.9 mmol/L, Cl 102 mmol/L, HCO3 24 mmol/L, Creatinine 68 μmol/L, eGFR >90. CRP 4 mg/L (normal, no bacterial infection). Interpretation: Mild leukocytosis likely stress response, normal eosinophils, no infection
investigations.other: ECG: Sinus tachycardia 118 bpm, normal axis, no acute ischaemic changes. PEFR monitoring: Baseline 180 L/min (40% predicted), post-salbutamol nebulizer 220 L/min (49% predicted, 22% improvement)

immediate: Oxygen therapy via Hudson mask to maintain SpO2 ≥94% (target 94-98% in acute asthma per TSANZ guidelines)
Salbutamol 5mg nebulized with oxygen, repeat every 20 minutes for 3 doses (or continuous nebulization if life-threatening features develop)
Ipratropium bromide 500mcg nebulized, can be given with salbutamol, repeat every 20 minutes for 3 doses
Prednisolone 50mg oral immediately (or hydrocortisone 100mg IV if unable to tolerate oral) - systemic corticosteroid essential in acute severe asthma
Consider IV magnesium sulfate 2g over 20 minutes if inadequate response to initial bronchodilators (evidence for severe asthma)
Continuous monitoring: SpO2, HR, RR, PEFR every 30 minutes
IV access and keep nil by mouth if deteriorating (preparation for potential intubation)
Senior medical review and consider ICU consultation if features of life-threatening asthma (PaCO2 rising, exhaustion, silent chest, altered conscious state)
short_term: Continue salbutamol nebulizers 4-6 hourly as response improves, wean frequency based on clinical improvement and PEFR
Prednisolone 50mg daily for 5-7 days (can stop abruptly, no taper needed for short course per eTG)
Monitor ABG 2-4 hours after initial treatment if PaCO2 was elevated or patient not improving (watch for rising CO2 indicating respiratory failure)
Chest physiotherapy input for airway clearance techniques
Asthma education - inhaler technique review with pharmacist or asthma nurse educator
Identify and address trigger factors (workplace assessment given school renovations)
Admit to hospital ward for minimum 24 hours observation (acute severe asthma requires admission per TSANZ guidelines)
long_term: Step up preventer therapy: Increase fluticasone/salmeterol to 500/50mcg BD or add additional controller (consider LAMA or leukotriene receptor antagonist)
Written Asthma Action Plan development prior to discharge (mandatory per National Asthma Council Australia guidelines)
GP follow-up within 2-7 days post-discharge for asthma review and spirometry when recovered
Respiratory physician referral for difficult-to-control asthma (2 admissions in 18 months indicates suboptimal control)
Allergy testing and consideration for allergen immunotherapy given dust mite allergy
Occupational health assessment regarding classroom trigger exposure, consider workplace modifications
Annual influenza vaccination (essential for asthma patients)
Smoking cessation support (patient non-smoker but reinforce importance of avoiding environmental tobacco smoke)
discharge_planning: Discharge criteria: PEFR >75% predicted or personal best, maintained for 24 hours; no bronchodilator use for 4 hours; SpO2 ≥94% on room air; patient can sleep without waking with asthma symptoms

Discharge medications: Continue fluticasone/salmeterol 250/25mcg 2 puffs BD (preventer), salbutamol 100mcg 2 puffs PRN (max 8 puffs/day), prednisolone 50mg daily for total 5 days, cetirizine 10mg daily
Provide spacer device for salbutamol delivery (more effective than puffer alone)
Provide peak flow meter for home PEFR monitoring
Written Asthma Action Plan with clear instructions on when to increase treatment, when to seek medical help, emergency contact numbers
GP appointment scheduled within 1 week
Patient education reinforced: inhaler technique, trigger avoidance, signs of deterioration, when to call ambulance (unable to speak, lips blue, collapse, no improvement with reliever)

marking_criteria.item: Takes focused asthma history including trigger identification, previous admissions/ICU, current medication use and adherence
Correctly assesses severity of asthma exacerbation using clinical features (inability to complete sentences, tachycardia >110, RR >30, PEFR <50% predicted = acute severe asthma)
Recognizes features suggesting life-threatening asthma (normal/rising PaCO2 in context of acute severe symptoms, exhaustion, silent chest, altered conscious state) and need for ICU consideration
Initiates appropriate first-line bronchodilator therapy: salbutamol nebulized 5mg (or 12 puffs via spacer) plus ipratropium 500mcg
Prescribes systemic corticosteroid at correct dose: prednisolone 50mg orally (or hydrocortisone 100mg IV) within first hour of presentation
Correctly interprets ABG showing Type 1 respiratory failure and recognizes significance of normal PaCO2 in severe asthma (indicates patient tiring)
Considers second-line therapy: IV magnesium sulfate 2g over 20 minutes for inadequate response to bronchodilators
Appropriately monitors patient with continuous SpO2, regular PEFR measurements, repeat ABG if deteriorating
Identifies need for hospital admission (acute severe asthma requires minimum 24 hours observation per TSANZ guidelines)
Plans appropriate discharge with Written Asthma Action Plan, inhaler technique review, GP follow-up, and step-up in preventer therapy
Demonstrates clear communication with patient about diagnosis, treatment plan, trigger avoidance, and warning signs of deterioration requiring emergency help

learning_objectives: Assess severity of acute asthma exacerbation using clinical features and objective measurements (PEFR, SpO2, ABG) per TSANZ guidelines
Differentiate acute severe, life-threatening, and near-fatal asthma based on clinical and investigation findings
Initiate appropriate emergency management of acute severe asthma: high-dose bronchodilators (salbutamol nebulized or via spacer, ipratropium), systemic corticosteroids, supplemental oxygen
Recognize indications for second-line therapy (IV magnesium sulfate) and ICU referral in acute asthma
Interpret arterial blood gas in acute asthma and recognize significance of normal/rising PaCO2 as indicator of respiratory failure

Develop appropriate discharge plan including Written Asthma Action Plan, inhaler technique education, trigger identification, and follow-up arrangements per National Asthma Council Australia recommendations

osces.title: COPD Acute Exacerbation with Type 2 Respiratory Failure - NIV Indication and Management

patient_scenario.chief_complaint: Worsening shortness of breath for 3 days, increased sputum production (green), confusion this morning
patient_scenario.history_presenting_illness: 68-year-old man with severe COPD (GOLD Stage 3) presenting with acute exacerbation. Baseline shortness of breath on minimal exertion (MRC dyspnoea scale 4 - stops for breath after walking 100 meters). Over past 3 days, progressive worsening of dyspnoea now present at rest, increased cough with green purulent sputum production (approximately 2 tablespoons per day, increased from usual white/clear sputum). No haemoptysis. No chest pain. Wife reports patient confused this morning, more drowsy than usual. Patient has had 3 COPD exacerbations in past 12 months requiring hospital admission, one requiring ICU admission for NIV 6 months ago. Current symptoms worse than previous exacerbations. Has been using home oxygen 2L/min for past 18 months. Using salbutamol and ipratropium nebulizers at home QID but increased to every 2 hours yesterday without improvement.
past_medical_history: COPD GOLD Stage 3 diagnosed 8 years ago (severe, FEV1 40% predicted)
Previous ICU admission 6 months ago for Type 2 respiratory failure requiring BiPAP ventilation for 48 hours
Ischaemic heart disease with previous myocardial infarction 4 years ago, 2 stents to LAD
Hypertension diagnosed 12 years ago, well controlled
Type 2 diabetes mellitus diagnosed 6 years ago, on oral hypoglycaemics

social_history.smoking: 60 pack-year history (1 pack/day for 40 years), quit 5 years ago after COPD diagnosis
social_history.alcohol: Previous heavy drinker (6-8 standard drinks daily), now abstinent for 4 years
social_history.exercise: Minimal - limited by severe dyspnoea, uses mobility scooter for shopping, housebound most days
social_history.occupation_detail: Retired construction worker, previous asbestos exposure in 1980s-90s (30 years in building industry). Lives with wife in single-storey house, requires assistance with ADLs

patient_scenario.family_history: Father died of lung cancer age 72 (heavy smoker), mother has hypertension. No family history of COPD or alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency

vital_signs.oxygen_saturation: 84% on 2L/min home oxygen via nasal prongs (usual baseline 90-92% on 2L/min)

examination_findings.respiratory: General inspection: Patient appears drowsy, GCS 14/15 (E4 V4 M6), responding to questions but slow, not oriented to time. Sitting upright in tripod position, pursed lip breathing. Cyanosed (blue lips and tongue indicating central cyanosis). Using accessory muscles of respiration. Barrel chest deformity consistent with hyperinflation. Inspection: Reduced chest expansion bilaterally, symmetrical. No scars. Prolonged expiratory phase. Palpation: Reduced chest expansion globally <3cm, tactile vocal fremitus reduced bilaterally. Percussion: Hyperresonant throughout both lung fields with loss of cardiac dullness (hyperinflation). Low position of diaphragm (percussion note changes from resonant to dull at 9th rib posteriorly, normally 7th rib). Auscultation: Bilateral wheeze throughout inspiration and expiration, coarse crackles at right lung base, prolonged expiratory phase (I:E ratio 1:3). Reduced air entry globally. Focal crackles right base suggest possible consolidation/infection
examination_findings.cardiovascular: Heart sounds dual, no murmurs. Tachycardic 102 bpm regular. JVP elevated 4cm above sternal angle (suggests cor pulmonale - right heart strain from chronic lung disease). Peripheral pulses present. Mild bilateral ankle oedema (pitting 1+) consistent with fluid retention from cor pulmonale. Capillary refill 2 seconds
examination_findings.other_systems: Abdomen soft, non-tender, no organomegaly, no ascites. Liver edge palpable 2cm below right costal margin (may be displaced down by hyperinflated lungs rather than true hepatomegaly). Neurological: GCS 14/15 as above, drowsy but rousable, no focal neurology, asterixis (flapping tremor) present bilaterally when arms extended (CO2 retention). Pupils equal and reactive. No papilloedema on fundoscopy

investigations.chest_xray: Hyperinflated lungs with flattened hemidiaphragms bilaterally, increased retrosternal airspace on lateral view. Prominent pulmonary arteries suggesting pulmonary hypertension. New focal opacity in right lower zone consistent with consolidation (suggesting infective exacerbation). No pneumothorax. No significant pleural effusion. Cardiac silhouette normal size but difficult to assess due to hyperinflation. Previous CXR 3 months ago showed hyperinflation without focal consolidation - new right lower zone change concerning for pneumonia precipitating COPD exacerbation
investigations.spirometry: Cannot be performed during acute exacerbation (unreliable and patient too unwell). Previous spirometry 4 months ago (when stable): FEV1 1.2L (40% predicted), FVC 3.0L (68% predicted), FEV1/FVC ratio 40% (normal >70%), consistent with severe COPD GOLD Stage 3. Post-bronchodilator FEV1 1.3L (minimal reversibility, typical for COPD). DLCO 45% predicted (impaired gas transfer)
investigations.blood_gas: Arterial blood gas on 2L/min oxygen via nasal prongs: pH 7.28 (acidotic), PaCO2 68 mmHg (hypercapnia, normal 35-45 mmHg), PaO2 54 mmHg (hypoxaemia, normal >80 mmHg), HCO3 32 mmol/L (elevated, metabolic compensation for chronic respiratory acidosis), Base excess +4, Lactate 2.1 mmol/L, SaO2 84%. Interpretation: Acute-on-chronic Type 2 respiratory failure (hypoxaemia + hypercapnia with respiratory acidosis pH <7.35). Elevated bicarbonate suggests chronic CO2 retention with renal compensation, but pH 7.28 indicates acute decompensation. This ABG meets criteria for NIV (pH 7.25-7.35 with hypercapnia per BTS/TSANZ guidelines)
investigations.bloods: Full blood count: Hb 158 g/L (elevated, secondary polycythaemia from chronic hypoxia), Haematocrit 0.52 (elevated), WCC 14.8 × 10⁹/L (neutrophils 12.1, lymphocytes 1.9, eosinophils 0.2) indicating infection, Platelets 256 × 10⁹/L. Electrolytes: Na 136 mmol/L, K 4.2 mmol/L, Cl 98 mmol/L, HCO3 32 mmol/L (matches ABG), Creatinine 124 μmol/L (elevated from baseline 98 μmol/L, likely dehydration), eGFR 48 mL/min/1.73m² (CKD stage 3a). Blood glucose 8.2 mmol/L. CRP 87 mg/L (markedly elevated, confirms bacterial infection). Troponin I 12 ng/L (mildly elevated, likely demand ischaemia from hypoxia, not acute coronary syndrome). Brain natriuretic peptide (BNP) 245 pg/mL (mildly elevated, consistent with cor pulmonale)
investigations.other: ECG: Sinus tachycardia 102 bpm, right axis deviation, tall peaked P waves in lead II (P pulmonale suggesting right atrial enlargement), no acute ischaemic changes. Sputum microscopy and culture sent: Gram stain shows abundant neutrophils and Gram-positive diplococci (suggestive Streptococcus pneumoniae), culture pending. Blood cultures × 2 sets sent (no growth at 48 hours)

immediate: Controlled oxygen therapy: Reduce oxygen to 1L/min via nasal prongs targeting SpO2 88-92% (NOT higher - risk of worsening hypercapnia in Type 2 respiratory failure). Venturi mask 24% or 28% preferable for precise FiO2

Commence non-invasive ventilation (NIV/BiPAP) immediately - patient meets criteria: pH 7.25-7.35, hypercapnia (PaCO2 >45 mmHg), respiratory acidosis despite controlled oxygen. NIV reduces need for intubation and mortality in COPD exacerbations with Type 2 respiratory failure

NIV settings: BiPAP mode, IPAP (inspiratory positive airway pressure) 18 cmH2O initially, EPAP (expiratory positive airway pressure) 4-5 cmH2O, FiO2 titrated to SpO2 88-92%. Full face mask interface (mouth breathers). Aim for 3-4 hours continuous initially
Nebulized bronchodilators: Salbutamol 5mg + ipratropium 500mcg every 4-6 hours (can be given via NIV circuit or brief breaks)
Systemic corticosteroid: Prednisolone 50mg orally daily (or hydrocortisone 100mg IV QID if nil by mouth). Short course 5-7 days reduces treatment failure and shortens hospital stay per eTG

Antibiotics for infective exacerbation (purulent sputum + CXR consolidation + elevated inflammatory markers): Amoxicillin-clavulanate 875/125mg PO TDS for 5 days OR if penicillin allergy: doxycycline 100mg PO BD. Choice per eTG for moderate-severe COPD exacerbation with pneumonia
IV access, fluid resuscitation with 0.9% NaCl 500mL over 4 hours (patient dehydrated, elevated creatinine), then maintenance fluids
Strict fluid balance monitoring (risk of fluid overload with cor pulmonale)
Continuous monitoring: SpO2, HR, BP, RR, telemetry. Repeat ABG 1-2 hours after NIV commencement to assess response (target pH improving >7.30, PaCO2 decreasing)
HDU/ICU admission for NIV monitoring (requires 1:2 nursing and continuous monitoring per hospital protocol)
Keep patient nil by mouth initially while on NIV (aspiration risk with full face mask)
short_term: Continue NIV for minimum 24 hours if responding (pH improving, PaCO2 decreasing, clinical improvement). Wean gradually with 'NIV-free' periods increasing if patient stable
Repeat ABG 1-2 hours after NIV commencement, then 4-6 hourly until pH >7.35 and PaCO2 stable

If NIV failure (pH <7.25 despite NIV, worsening hypercapnia, exhaustion, unable to tolerate NIV, decreasing GCS): discuss intubation and invasive ventilation with ICU team and patient/family. Consider ceiling of care discussion given severe COPD and previous ICU admission
Continue prednisolone 50mg daily for 5 days total (stop abruptly, no taper needed per eTG)
Complete 5-day course amoxicillin-clavulanate (or doxycycline if penicillin allergy)
Wean oxygen as able, targeting SpO2 88-92% (patient on long-term oxygen therapy, baseline 90-92%)
Monitor electrolytes daily (risk hypokalaemia with salbutamol and prednisolone)
Chest physiotherapy for sputum clearance once patient stable enough to participate
Assess for cor pulmonale: consider echocardiography to assess right ventricular function and pulmonary artery pressure
Smoking cessation reinforcement (patient quit 5 years ago, ensure no relapse)
long_term: COPD exacerbation prevention: Ensure optimized inhaler therapy (currently on LAMA + LABA/ICS combination - appropriate for GOLD Stage 3 with frequent exacerbations)
Pulmonary rehabilitation referral (shown to reduce admissions and improve quality of life in severe COPD)
Annual influenza vaccination and pneumococcal vaccination if not up to date (reduces exacerbation frequency)

Home oxygen assessment: Patient already on LTOT (long-term oxygen therapy) 2L/min, confirm prescription still appropriate. Repeat ABG on room air when stable to assess ongoing oxygen needs (LTOT indicated if PaO2 <55 mmHg on room air, or PaO2 <60 mmHg with cor pulmonale/polycythaemia)

Advance care planning discussion given severe COPD with recurrent admissions and ICU requirement. Document ceiling of care, resuscitation status, and patient wishes for future exacerbations (consider respiratory-assisted Advance Care Directive)
Respiratory physician outpatient follow-up 4-6 weeks post-discharge for COPD review
Consider domiciliary NIV (home BiPAP at night) if persistent hypercapnia when stable - some evidence for benefit in selected severe COPD patients with chronic Type 2 respiratory failure
Address comorbidities: Continue cardiac medications (aspirin, statin, ACE inhibitor for IHD), optimize diabetes control (HbA1c target <7% or 53 mmol/mol), monitor renal function (CKD stage 3a)
Social supports: Discuss with patient and family regarding home care needs, consider referral to aged care assessment team (ACAT) for home care package if ADL support needed
discharge_planning: Discharge criteria: pH >7.35 on ABG, PaCO2 returned to baseline (or stable chronic elevation if known), SpO2 88-92% on baseline oxygen, clinically improving (RR <25, HR <100), tolerating oral intake, mobilizing safely, completed minimum 3 days antibiotics and corticosteroids, inhaler technique reviewed

Discharge medications: Tiotropium 18mcg 2 puffs daily, fluticasone/salmeterol 500/50mcg 2 puffs BD, salbutamol 5mg nebules QID PRN (supply 1 month), ipratropium 500mcg nebules QID PRN (supply 1 month), continue aspirin 100mg daily, atorvastatin 40mg nocte, perindopril 5mg daily, metformin 1000mg BD, prednisolone 50mg daily for total 5 days then stop, amoxicillin-clavulanate 875/125mg TDS for total 5 days
Continue home oxygen 2L/min continuous (15 hours/day minimum per LTOT guidelines). Reinforce with patient: DO NOT increase oxygen without medical advice (risk worsening hypercapnia)
Provide written COPD Action Plan (similar to asthma action plan) with instructions on recognizing exacerbation, when to increase bronchodilators, when to seek medical help, emergency contacts
Supply home nebulizer for salbutamol and ipratropium delivery (patient already has nebulizer at home)
Arrange respiratory nurse specialist home visit within 48 hours of discharge to check oxygen equipment, inhaler technique, monitor for early deterioration
GP appointment within 1 week for post-discharge review
Respiratory physician outpatient appointment in 4-6 weeks
Provide patient information sheet on COPD exacerbation warning signs and when to call ambulance (confusion, severe breathlessness, blue lips)

marking_criteria.item: Takes focused COPD history including baseline functional status (MRC dyspnoea scale), exacerbation frequency, previous ICU admissions, smoking history, and home oxygen use
Correctly interprets ABG showing acute-on-chronic Type 2 respiratory failure (pH 7.28, PaCO2 68 mmHg, elevated HCO3 indicating chronic compensation) and recognizes indication for NIV
Initiates controlled oxygen therapy targeting SpO2 88-92% (NOT 94-98% as in non-COPD patients) to prevent worsening hypercapnia in Type 2 respiratory failure
Commences non-invasive ventilation (BiPAP) with appropriate settings (IPAP 18, EPAP 4-5) for patient meeting NIV criteria (pH 7.25-7.35, hypercapnia, respiratory acidosis)

Prescribes appropriate antibiotics for infective COPD exacerbation with consolidation: amoxicillin-clavulanate 875/125mg TDS for 5 days per eTG (covers Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae)
Prescribes systemic corticosteroid: prednisolone 50mg daily for 5-7 days (reduces treatment failure and shortens hospital stay per Cochrane review)
Recognizes features of cor pulmonale (elevated JVP, peripheral oedema, right axis deviation on ECG, elevated BNP) as complication of severe COPD requiring specific management
Plans appropriate monitoring: repeat ABG 1-2 hours post-NIV to assess response, continuous SpO2/HR/RR monitoring, identifies NIV failure criteria (pH <7.25, worsening hypercapnia, exhaustion)
Discusses ceiling of care and advance care planning given severe COPD with recurrent admissions and ICU requirement (appropriate for patient with life-limiting disease)
Plans appropriate long-term management: pulmonary rehabilitation, optimized inhaler therapy, LTOT review, influenza/pneumococcal vaccination, respiratory physician follow-up
Provides clear discharge plan with COPD Action Plan, inhaler technique review, home oxygen safety education, and early follow-up arrangements

learning_objectives: Identify Type 2 respiratory failure on ABG (hypoxaemia + hypercapnia + respiratory acidosis) and distinguish acute-on-chronic from acute Type 2 respiratory failure based on pH and bicarbonate levels
Apply controlled oxygen therapy principles in COPD with Type 2 respiratory failure (target SpO2 88-92%) to prevent worsening hypercapnia
Recognize indications for non-invasive ventilation (NIV) in acute COPD exacerbation (pH 7.25-7.35 with hypercapnia and respiratory acidosis despite controlled oxygen) per BTS/TSANZ guidelines
Initiate and monitor NIV with appropriate settings (BiPAP: IPAP 18, EPAP 4-5) and recognize criteria for NIV failure requiring intubation
Prescribe evidence-based treatment for infective COPD exacerbation: antibiotics (amoxicillin-clavulanate per eTG), systemic corticosteroids (prednisolone 50mg for 5 days), and bronchodilators
Identify complications of severe COPD including cor pulmonale, secondary polycythaemia, and chronic respiratory failure requiring long-term oxygen therapy
Plan appropriate long-term COPD management including pulmonary rehabilitation, vaccination, advance care planning, and specialist respiratory follow-up

osces.title: Community-Acquired Pneumonia - CURB-65 Severity Assessment and Antibiotic Selection

patient_scenario.chief_complaint: Fever, productive cough with yellow-green sputum, right-sided chest pain for 4 days, worsening shortness of breath
patient_scenario.history_presenting_illness: 74-year-old woman presenting with 4-day history of productive cough, fever, and right-sided pleuritic chest pain. Symptoms began gradually with dry cough and mild fever (subjective, no thermometer at home). Over 48 hours, cough became productive of yellow-green sputum (approximately 1-2 tablespoons daily). Developed sharp right-sided chest pain worse on deep inspiration and coughing (pleuritic pain). Yesterday noticed increasing shortness of breath at rest. No haemoptysis. Reduced oral intake over past 2 days due to fatigue and nausea. No recent travel. No sick contacts. Had influenza vaccination 5 months ago (May 2025). No previous pneumococcal vaccination. Usually independent with ADLs, lives alone in own home. Daughter visited yesterday and brought patient to ED due to concern about deterioration.
past_medical_history: Hypertension diagnosed 15 years ago, well controlled
Osteoarthritis of knees, bilateral knee replacements (left 2018, right 2020)
Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease (GORD) diagnosed 8 years ago
No previous pneumonia, no chronic lung disease

social_history.alcohol: Occasional glass of wine with dinner, approximately 3 standard drinks per week
social_history.exercise: Daily walks 30 minutes prior to illness, now unable to walk to letterbox without dyspnoea
social_history.occupation_detail: Retired librarian (retired 9 years ago at age 65). Lives alone in single-storey house, independent with ADLs, drives car. Daughter lives 15 minutes away and visits twice weekly. Active in local book club and church community

patient_scenario.family_history: Father died of myocardial infarction age 68 (heavy smoker), mother died of stroke age 82. No family history of lung disease or cancer

examination_findings.respiratory: General inspection: Elderly woman appearing mildly unwell and tired, flushed, breathing comfortably at rest but mildly tachypnoeic. Able to speak in full sentences. No cyanosis. Inspection: Reduced chest expansion on right side compared to left. No scars. Palpation: Reduced chest expansion right lower zone, increased tactile vocal fremitus over right lower zone posteriorly (consolidation). Percussion: Dull percussion note over right lower zone posteriorly (consolidation), resonant elsewhere. Auscultation: Bronchial breathing over right lower zone posteriorly with coarse inspiratory crackles, vocal resonance increased (patient says 'ninety-nine' sounds louder over affected area - aegophony present). Left lung clear. No wheeze. Pleural rub not appreciated
examination_findings.cardiovascular: Heart sounds I + II, no murmurs. Regular rhythm 96 bpm. JVP not elevated. Peripheral pulses present and equal. Capillary refill <2 seconds. No peripheral oedema
examination_findings.other_systems: Abdomen soft and non-tender, no organomegaly, no masses. Bowel sounds present. Neurological: Alert and oriented to person, place, time. GCS 15/15. No focal neurology. Abbreviated Mental Test Score (AMTS) 9/10 (lost 1 point for not recalling year correctly - said 2024 instead of 2025, otherwise fully oriented). No confusion. Skin: Warm and dry, no rash

investigations.chest_xray: Posteroanterior and lateral CXR: Right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms, well-defined opacity obscuring right hemidiaphragm and right heart border. Silhouette sign positive (right heart border obscured suggests right middle lobe or lingula involvement, but opacity more basal suggests right lower lobe). No pleural effusion. No pneumothorax. Cardiomediastinal contour normal. Left lung clear. No cavitation. No hilar lymphadenopathy. Interpretation: Community-acquired pneumonia, right lower lobe, moderate severity
investigations.spirometry: Not performed during acute illness (not indicated in acute pneumonia)
investigations.blood_gas: Not performed (SpO2 92% on room air does not meet criteria for ABG - would perform if SpO2 <90% or severe respiratory distress)
investigations.bloods: Full blood count: Hb 128 g/L (normal for age), WCC 15.6 × 10⁹/L (neutrophils 13.2, lymphocytes 1.8, eosinophils 0.1) indicating bacterial infection, Platelets 298 × 10⁹/L. Electrolytes: Na 132 mmol/L (mild hyponatraemia, common in pneumonia), K 4.1 mmol/L, Cl 98 mmol/L, HCO3 24 mmol/L, Urea 8.2 mmol/L (mildly elevated, dehydration), Creatinine 86 μmol/L (normal for age), eGFR 64 mL/min/1.73m² (CKD stage 2, age-related). Blood glucose 6.2 mmol/L (normal). CRP 142 mg/L (markedly elevated, confirms bacterial infection). Albumin 36 g/L (low-normal). Liver function tests: Bilirubin 12 μmol/L, ALT 28 U/L, ALP 78 U/L, GGT 32 U/L (all normal)
investigations.other: Sputum microscopy: Abundant neutrophils, Gram-positive diplococci seen (suggestive Streptococcus pneumoniae - most common cause of CAP). Sputum culture pending (results in 48-72 hours). Blood cultures × 2 sets sent prior to antibiotics (no growth at 48 hours). Pneumococcal urinary antigen test: Positive (confirms Streptococcus pneumoniae as causative organism - test rapid, results same day). Legionella urinary antigen test: Negative. CURB-65 score calculation: Confusion (AMTS <8) = 0 (patient scored 9/10, not confused), Urea >7 mmol/L = 1 (urea 8.2), Respiratory rate ≥30/min = 0 (RR 24), Blood pressure (systolic <90 or diastolic ≤60) = 1 (BP 108/64, systolic >90 but borderline), Age ≥65 = 1 (age 74). Total CURB-65 score = 2-3 (depending on interpretation of BP). Score 2 = moderate risk, consider hospital admission; Score 3 = high risk, requires hospital admission, consider ICU if deteriorating

immediate: Admit to hospital medical ward (CURB-65 score 2-3 indicates moderate-high risk, requires inpatient management per eTG and Therapeutic Guidelines)
Supplemental oxygen via nasal prongs 2-3L/min to maintain SpO2 ≥94% (target 94-98% in non-COPD patient with pneumonia)
IV access (16-18G cannula) for fluid resuscitation and IV antibiotics
IV fluid resuscitation: 0.9% sodium chloride 1L over 4 hours initially (patient dehydrated - elevated urea, reduced oral intake, borderline BP), then reassess. Aim for urine output >30 mL/hr

Empirical IV antibiotics for moderate-severe community-acquired pneumonia per eTG: Benzylpenicillin 1.2g (2.4 million units) IV Q6H PLUS doxycycline 100mg PO BD. Rationale: Benzylpenicillin covers Streptococcus pneumoniae (confirmed on urinary antigen), doxycycline provides atypical coverage (Mycoplasma, Chlamydia, Legionella). If penicillin allergy: moxifloxacin 400mg IV daily
Regular antipyretics: Paracetamol 1g PO QID for fever and pleuritic pain
Venous thromboembolism (VTE) prophylaxis: Enoxaparin 40mg SC daily (patient admitted, reduced mobility, age >60 = moderate VTE risk)
Monitor vital signs 4-hourly initially: BP, HR, RR, temperature, SpO2
Strict fluid balance chart (input/output monitoring)
Chest physiotherapy referral for breathing exercises and airway clearance
short_term: Continue IV benzylpenicillin 1.2g Q6H + doxycycline 100mg BD for minimum 48-72 hours until clinically improving (afebrile for 24 hours, improving respiratory symptoms, stable vital signs)

Switch to oral antibiotics when able (sequential therapy): Amoxicillin 1g TDS PO + doxycycline 100mg BD PO to complete total 5-7 days therapy (eTG recommends minimum 5 days, extend to 7 days for moderate-severe pneumonia)
Monitor inflammatory markers: Repeat CRP on day 3-4 (should be declining if responding to treatment, failure to improve suggests treatment failure or complications)
Repeat CXR only if clinically deteriorating or not improving by day 3-4 (routine CXR not needed if improving clinically)
Daily urea and electrolytes to monitor for resolving hyponatraemia and improving hydration (urea should decrease with IV fluids)
Wean oxygen as tolerated, aiming for SpO2 ≥94% on room air before discharge
Monitor for complications: Pleural effusion (new dullness, reduced air entry), empyema (persistent fever despite antibiotics), sepsis (hypotension, confusion, organ dysfunction)
Mobilize patient early once stable (reduces VTE risk, prevents deconditioning)
Ensure adequate nutrition and hydration (oral intake encouraged once nausea resolves)
long_term: Pneumococcal vaccination prior to discharge: Administer 23-valent pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccine (23vPPV) to prevent future pneumococcal pneumonia (indicated for all adults ≥65 years and younger adults with risk factors)

Repeat CXR at 6 weeks post-discharge to confirm radiological resolution (important in patients >50 years to exclude underlying malignancy - up to 10% of pneumonias in this age group have underlying lung cancer)
GP follow-up within 1 week of discharge for clinical review
Review comorbidities: Hypertension management (BP was low during admission, may need medication adjustment), GORD management (continue omeprazole)
Smoking cessation counselling (patient non-smoker, reinforce importance)
Consider frailty assessment given age 74 and recent acute illness (may benefit from comprehensive geriatric assessment if functional decline noted)
Discuss advance care planning if appropriate (patient currently well, but age 74 with acute illness is opportunity to document wishes)
discharge_planning: Discharge criteria: Afebrile for 24 hours, respiratory rate <24/min, heart rate <100 bpm, SpO2 ≥94% on room air, able to take oral fluids and medications, systolic BP >90 mmHg, completed minimum 3 days IV antibiotics with clinical improvement

Discharge medications: Amoxicillin 1g TDS for 5-7 days total (continue oral to complete course), doxycycline 100mg BD for 5-7 days total, irbesartan 150mg daily (may need dose review with GP), amlodipine 5mg daily, omeprazole 20mg daily, paracetamol 1g QID PRN
Pneumococcal vaccine administered (23vPPV) - patient education on one-off vaccine for pneumonia prevention
Safety netting advice: Seek medical attention if fever returns, worsening breathlessness, coughing blood, chest pain, confusion. Call ambulance if severe breathlessness or collapse
Arrange CXR at GP practice or radiology clinic in 6 weeks (provide radiology referral)
GP appointment within 1 week for review of blood pressure, electrolytes, and clinical recovery
Patient information leaflet on pneumonia recovery (may take 4-6 weeks to feel fully recovered, fatigue common for several weeks)
Discuss with daughter regarding short-term support at home if needed (meals, shopping, transport to appointments)
Cease enoxaparin on discharge (VTE prophylaxis only needed during hospital admission, not post-discharge for pneumonia)

marking_criteria.item: Takes focused history including symptom timeline, sputum characteristics, pleuritic chest pain, reduced oral intake, and identifies pneumonia risk factors (age, vaccination status)
Performs systematic respiratory examination identifying key signs of consolidation (dull percussion, bronchial breathing, increased vocal resonance/tactile fremitus, crackles)

Correctly calculates CURB-65 score (Confusion, Urea >7, RR ≥30, BP systolic <90 or diastolic ≤60, Age ≥65) and interprets score to guide admission decision (score 2-3 = moderate-high risk requiring hospital admission)
Interprets CXR findings of right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms, recognizing pattern consistent with bacterial community-acquired pneumonia
Prescribes appropriate empirical antibiotics for moderate-severe CAP per eTG: Benzylpenicillin 1.2g IV Q6H PLUS doxycycline 100mg BD (covers typical and atypical organisms)
Initiates supportive care: IV fluid resuscitation for dehydration, supplemental oxygen targeting SpO2 ≥94%, regular antipyretics, VTE prophylaxis
Recognizes positive pneumococcal urinary antigen test confirms Streptococcus pneumoniae as causative organism (most common cause of CAP, guides antibiotic choice)
Plans appropriate monitoring: Vital signs, fluid balance, repeat CRP to assess response, repeat CXR only if not improving clinically
Administers pneumococcal vaccination (23vPPV) prior to discharge for secondary prevention in patient ≥65 years who has not previously received pneumococcal vaccine
Arranges 6-week follow-up CXR to confirm radiological resolution and exclude underlying malignancy (important in patients >50 years with pneumonia)
Provides clear discharge plan with oral antibiotics to complete course, safety netting advice, GP follow-up, and CXR appointment

learning_objectives: Apply CURB-65 severity score to assess community-acquired pneumonia and guide admission decisions (score 0-1 outpatient, 2 consider admission, 3-5 hospital admission +/- ICU)
Identify clinical signs of pulmonary consolidation on examination (dull percussion, bronchial breathing, increased vocal resonance, tactile fremitus, coarse crackles)
Interpret chest X-ray findings of pneumonia (lobar consolidation, air bronchograms, silhouette sign) and recognize patterns of bacterial vs atypical pneumonia
Select appropriate empirical antibiotics for community-acquired pneumonia per eTG based on severity and local resistance patterns (benzylpenicillin + doxycycline for moderate-severe CAP)
Recognize Streptococcus pneumoniae as most common cause of CAP and interpret pneumococcal urinary antigen test
Plan appropriate supportive care for pneumonia (oxygen, IV fluids, VTE prophylaxis) and monitoring to detect complications (empyema, effusion, sepsis)
Implement secondary prevention strategies: Pneumococcal vaccination (23vPPV for adults ≥65 years), influenza vaccination annually
Arrange appropriate follow-up including 6-week CXR to confirm resolution and exclude underlying lung cancer in patients >50 years

Therapeutic Guidelines - Antibiotic: Community-acquired pneumonia severity assessment and management
TSANZ (Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand) - CAP guidelines
Australian Immunisation Handbook - Pneumococcal vaccination recommendations
CURB-65 pneumonia severity score - British Thoracic Society (adapted for Australian practice)

osces.title: Pulmonary Embolism - Wells Score, D-dimer Interpretation, and Anticoagulation Management

patient_scenario.chief_complaint: Sudden-onset right-sided chest pain and shortness of breath 6 hours ago, worse on deep breathing, coughing up small amount of blood
patient_scenario.history_presenting_illness: 42-year-old woman presenting with acute onset pleuritic chest pain and dyspnoea. Symptoms began suddenly this morning (6 hours ago) while at work - sharp right-sided chest pain that worsens with deep inspiration and coughing. Associated shortness of breath at rest, worse on exertion (unable to climb one flight of stairs without stopping). One episode of haemoptysis 2 hours ago - small amount of bright red blood mixed with sputum (approximately 1 teaspoon). No preceding trauma. No recent viral illness. No calf pain or swelling reported initially, but on direct questioning admits right calf has felt 'tight' for past 3 days. Significant risk factors: Long-haul flight from Australia to London 8 days ago (20+ hours flying time with minimal movement, slept most of flight). Currently taking oral contraceptive pill (combined oestrogen-progesterone formulation) for past 6 years. No previous VTE. No family history of clotting disorders. No recent surgery. Not pregnant (last menstrual period 2 weeks ago).

social_history.alcohol: Social drinker, 4-6 standard drinks per week
social_history.exercise: Regular gym 3 times per week, otherwise sedentary desk job (software developer, sits 8-10 hours daily)
social_history.occupation_detail: Software developer working from home most days, recently returned from work trip to London (attended 5-day conference, long-haul flights). Single, lives alone in apartment. No children

patient_scenario.family_history: Mother alive and well, father has hypertension. No family history of venous thromboembolism (VTE), pulmonary embolism (PE), deep vein thrombosis (DVT), or known thrombophilia (Factor V Leiden, Protein C/S deficiency, antiphospholipid syndrome)

examination_findings.respiratory: General inspection: Patient appears anxious and mildly dyspnoeic, able to speak in full sentences but tachypnoeic. No cyanosis. No use of accessory muscles. Inspection: Chest expansion symmetrical, no scars, no obvious deformity. Respiratory rate 26/min. Palpation: Chest expansion equal bilaterally, no tenderness over chest wall, tactile fremitus normal bilaterally. Percussion: Resonant throughout both lung fields, no dullness. Auscultation: Vesicular breath sounds bilaterally, no wheeze, no crackles, no focal signs of consolidation. Pleural rub not appreciated (can be present in PE with pleural involvement). Normal air entry throughout. Respiratory examination essentially normal - absence of focal signs does NOT exclude PE
examination_findings.cardiovascular: Heart sounds I + II present, no murmurs. Loud P2 (pulmonary component of second heart sound) suggesting pulmonary hypertension. Tachycardia 108 bpm regular. JVP normal (not elevated - massive PE would show elevated JVP). Peripheral pulses present and equal. Capillary refill <2 seconds. No peripheral oedema of ankles. RIGHT CALF examination: Right calf diameter 2cm larger than left calf (measured 10cm below tibial tuberosity), right calf tender on palpation, positive Homan's sign (calf pain on passive dorsiflexion of foot - low sensitivity/specificity but supportive of DVT). No erythema, calf warm to touch. Left calf normal. Findings suggestive of right leg DVT
examination_findings.other_systems: Abdomen soft and non-tender, no organomegaly, no masses. Neurological: Alert and oriented, GCS 15/15, no focal neurology, no signs of stroke (PE can cause paradoxical embolism via PFO)

investigations.chest_xray: Posteroanterior CXR: Normal cardiac size. Clear lung fields bilaterally. No focal consolidation. No pleural effusion. No pneumothorax. Hemidiaphragms normal. No pulmonary oedema. Interpretation: Normal CXR does NOT exclude pulmonary embolism (CXR normal in 20-40% of PE cases). CXR primarily useful to exclude alternative diagnoses (pneumothorax, pneumonia, heart failure). Classic PE signs on CXR (Westermark sign - oligaemia, Hampton's hump - wedge-shaped opacity, Fleischner sign - enlarged pulmonary artery) are RARE and non-specific
investigations.spirometry: Not performed (not indicated in acute PE assessment)
investigations.blood_gas: Arterial blood gas on room air: pH 7.46 (respiratory alkalosis from hyperventilation), PaCO2 32 mmHg (hypocapnia from tachypnoea), PaO2 68 mmHg (hypoxaemia), HCO3 22 mmol/L (normal), Base excess -1, SaO2 94%, A-a gradient 38 mmHg (elevated, normal <15 mmHg - indicates V/Q mismatch from PE). Lactate 1.2 mmol/L (normal). Interpretation: Type 1 respiratory failure (hypoxaemia without hypercapnia) with respiratory alkalosis and increased A-a gradient, consistent with pulmonary embolism. However, normal ABG does NOT exclude PE
investigations.bloods: Full blood count: Hb 136 g/L, WCC 8.9 × 10⁹/L (normal), Platelets 245 × 10⁹/L (normal - important baseline before anticoagulation). Electrolytes: Na 139 mmol/L, K 4.0 mmol/L, Creatinine 64 μmol/L, eGFR >90 (normal renal function - important for DOAC dosing). CRP 12 mg/L (mildly elevated, common in PE). Troponin I 45 ng/L (mildly elevated, suggests right ventricular strain from PE - negative prognostic indicator). BNP 285 pg/mL (elevated, indicates right ventricular dysfunction). D-dimer: 2,850 ng/mL (markedly elevated, normal <500 ng/mL). D-dimer high sensitivity but low specificity - elevated in PE, DVT, infection, malignancy, pregnancy, post-operative state, elderly. Negative D-dimer with low/moderate Wells score effectively excludes PE, but positive D-dimer requires imaging confirmation
investigations.other: Wells Score for Pulmonary Embolism calculation: Clinical signs/symptoms of DVT (right calf swelling, tenderness) = 3 points; PE most likely diagnosis (no alternative diagnosis more likely than PE) = 3 points; Heart rate >100 bpm (108 bpm) = 1.5 points; Immobilization ≥3 days or surgery in previous 4 weeks = 0 (recent flight but not immobilized 3+ consecutive days); Previous PE/DVT = 0 (no prior VTE); Haemoptysis = 1 point; Malignancy = 0 (no active cancer). TOTAL Wells Score = 3 + 3 + 1.5 + 1 = 8.5 points (HIGH probability, score >6). CT pulmonary angiogram (CTPA): Multiple filling defects in right lower lobe segmental and subsegmental pulmonary arteries consistent with pulmonary emboli. Right ventricular dilatation with RV/LV diameter ratio 1.2 (normal <1.0, indicates RV strain - intermediate-high risk PE). No evidence of right heart thrombus. Small right pleural effusion. Peripheral wedge-shaped opacity in right lower lobe (pulmonary infarction). Incidental note: Small PFO (patent foramen ovale) seen on contrast study. Lower limb venous duplex ultrasound: Acute DVT in right popliteal and posterior tibial veins (non-occlusive thrombus), compressibility reduced, no flow on Doppler. Left leg normal. Confirms source of PE. ECG: Sinus tachycardia 108 bpm, S1Q3T3 pattern (deep S wave in lead I, Q wave and inverted T wave in lead III - classic but insensitive ECG finding in PE, present in only 20% of cases), right axis deviation, right bundle branch block (RBBB). ECG changes suggest right heart strain from acute PE

immediate: Immediate anticoagulation: Start treatment-dose anticoagulation without waiting for CTPA if high clinical suspicion (Wells score 8.5 = high probability PE). Options: (1) Low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH) enoxaparin 1.5mg/kg SC once daily OR enoxaparin 1mg/kg SC BD, OR (2) Unfractionated heparin (UFH) IV infusion if patient unstable or high bleeding risk (can be rapidly reversed), OR (3) Direct oral anticoagulant (DOAC) - rivaroxaban 15mg BD or apixaban 10mg BD (loading dose regimen)

CHOICE for this patient: Rivaroxaban 15mg PO BD for 21 days (loading phase), then 20mg daily (maintenance). Rationale: Oral administration, no need for LMWH bridge, patient haemodynamically stable, normal renal function (eGFR >90), no contraindications. eTG first-line recommendation for acute PE
Supplemental oxygen via nasal prongs 2-4L/min to maintain SpO2 ≥94% (patient currently 94% on room air, may need oxygen with exertion)
Analgesia for pleuritic chest pain: Paracetamol 1g PO QID +/- low-dose oxycodone 5mg PO Q6H PRN if severe pain (NSAIDs relatively contraindicated with anticoagulation due to bleeding risk)

Cease oral contraceptive pill immediately (major VTE risk factor - oestrogen-containing contraceptives increase VTE risk 3-4 fold). Discuss alternative contraception (progesterone-only pill, Mirena IUD, barrier methods). NEVER restart combined OCP in patient with provoked or unprovoked VTE
IV access for potential resuscitation if patient deteriorates (patient currently stable but PE can rapidly worsen)
Continuous monitoring: Telemetry, SpO2, BP, HR, RR Q1-2H initially. Admit to monitored bed (high-dependency unit or medical ward with telemetry)

Risk stratification: Patient has intermediate-high risk PE (RV dysfunction on CTPA with RV/LV ratio >1.0, elevated troponin, elevated BNP). Consider thrombolysis if deteriorates (hypotension, worsening hypoxia, cardiac arrest)
Nil by mouth initially pending assessment for potential thrombolysis if patient deteriorates
short_term: Continue rivaroxaban 15mg BD for 21 days (loading dose), then reduce to rivaroxaban 20mg daily (maintenance dose) from day 22 onwards

Monitor for bleeding complications: Daily FBC to check Hb/platelets, check for signs of bleeding (haemoptysis, haematuria, melaena, ecchymoses). No routine INR monitoring needed with DOAC (unlike warfarin)
Repeat troponin and BNP at 24-48 hours: Declining levels indicate improving RV function, persistent elevation suggests ongoing RV strain

Echocardiography within 24-48 hours to assess RV function, RV dilatation, pulmonary artery pressure (intermediate-high risk PE requires echo to guide management and prognosis). Document presence of PFO

Mobilize patient as tolerated once anticoagulated and haemodynamically stable (early mobilization safe and reduces hospital stay, graduated compression stockings NOT routinely recommended per latest guidelines)

Thrombophilia screening: Indicated in this case (young patient age 42, provoked VTE by flight + OCP but consider testing for hereditary thrombophilia if family history or recurrent VTE). Test for Factor V Leiden, Prothrombin G20210A mutation, Protein C/S deficiency, Antithrombin deficiency, Antiphospholipid antibodies. Testing should be done AFTER completing anticoagulation (results affected by acute VTE and anticoagulants)
Consider inferior vena cava (IVC) filter only if absolute contraindication to anticoagulation (active bleeding) or recurrent PE despite therapeutic anticoagulation (NOT indicated in this patient)
Patient education: Anticoagulation compliance, bleeding risk signs, when to seek help (severe bleeding, worsening dyspnoea, chest pain, syncope)
Occupational health discussion: Long-haul flight VTE prevention (adequate hydration, regular leg exercises, aisle walking every 2 hours, consider compression stockings for future flights >4 hours)
long_term: Duration of anticoagulation: Minimum 3 months for provoked PE (clear trigger: long-haul flight + OCP). Consider extended anticoagulation (indefinite treatment) if: (1) Unprovoked PE, (2) Recurrent VTE, (3) Active cancer, (4) High-risk thrombophilia (homozygous Factor V Leiden, antiphospholipid syndrome). This patient has PROVOKED PE (flight + OCP) → treat for 3-6 months, then reassess. If thrombophilia screen positive, may extend duration

Contraception counselling: NEVER restart combined oral contraceptive pill (absolute contraindication after VTE). Discuss safe alternatives: Progesterone-only pill (Cerazette), Mirena IUD (levonorgestrel), Implanon (etonogestrel implant), barrier methods. Avoid all oestrogen-containing contraceptives (combined pill, vaginal ring, transdermal patch)
Repeat CTPA at 3 months to assess clot resolution (not routinely needed if patient clinically well, but can guide duration of anticoagulation if considering stopping at 3 months)

Long-term sequelae screening: Chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension (CTEPH) occurs in 2-4% of PE patients. If persistent dyspnoea, reduced exercise tolerance, or elevated pulmonary artery pressure on echo at 3 months → refer to respiratory/cardiology for V/Q scan and right heart catheterization to assess for CTEPH
Haematology outpatient follow-up at 3 months to review thrombophilia results, assess need for extended anticoagulation, discuss duration of treatment
Annual review with GP: Monitor for post-PE syndrome (persistent dyspnoea, exercise intolerance, reduced QOL), assess cardiovascular risk factors
Advise patient to inform all healthcare providers of VTE history (relevant for future surgery, hormonal contraception, pregnancy planning - anticoagulation needs adjustment)

Pregnancy planning counselling (if considering future pregnancy): Switch from DOAC to LMWH (DOACs contraindicated in pregnancy), prophylactic LMWH throughout pregnancy and 6 weeks postpartum (pregnancy is high VTE risk state, especially with prior VTE)
discharge_planning: Discharge criteria: Haemodynamically stable (BP >100 systolic, HR <100, RR <24), SpO2 ≥94% on room air or minimal oxygen, pain controlled with oral analgesia, tolerating oral anticoagulant, no evidence of bleeding, safe home environment with support

Discharge medications: Rivaroxaban 15mg BD for 21 days, then 20mg daily ongoing (minimum 3 months, review at haematology clinic). Paracetamol 1g QID PRN for pain. Cease Microgynon 30 (OCP) - do not restart. Provide 3 months supply of rivaroxaban with repeat prescriptions

Patient education materials: Written information on PE, anticoagulation (what is rivaroxaban, why taking it, duration, bleeding risks, drug interactions), signs of recurrent PE or DVT, when to call ambulance (severe breathlessness, chest pain, coughing blood, collapse)

Bleeding precautions advice: Avoid NSAIDs (use paracetamol for pain), use soft toothbrush, electric razor, avoid contact sports, seek medical attention if prolonged bleeding, unusual bruising, blood in urine/stool, severe headache

VTE prevention for future flights: Avoid flights >4 hours in first 3 months of treatment, after that: adequate hydration, regular leg exercises, aisle walking every 2 hours, consider compression stockings (20-30 mmHg), take rivaroxaban as usual, avoid alcohol excess
Provide patient alert card for anticoagulation (carry at all times, states taking rivaroxaban for PE, emergency contact information)
GP appointment within 1 week for review and blood test follow-up (FBC, renal function)
Haematology outpatient appointment in 3 months for thrombophilia results review and anticoagulation duration discussion
Contraception follow-up: GP or family planning clinic within 2 weeks to discuss and initiate alternative contraception (progesterone-only options)

Provide radiology referral for lower limb venous duplex ultrasound in 1 week to assess DVT progression (ensure clot not extending, though this doesn't usually change management if already anticoagulated)

marking_criteria.item: Takes focused history identifying VTE risk factors (long-haul flight, combined oral contraceptive pill, sedentary occupation) and symptoms suggesting PE (pleuritic chest pain, dyspnoea, haemoptysis) and DVT (calf tightness)
Correctly calculates Wells Score for Pulmonary Embolism (clinical DVT signs = 3, PE most likely = 3, HR >100 = 1.5, haemoptysis = 1) giving score 8.5 (HIGH probability, requires immediate imaging)
Interprets D-dimer correctly: Elevated D-dimer (2,850 ng/mL) in high Wells score patient requires CTPA confirmation (D-dimer alone cannot diagnose PE, imaging essential)
Recognizes CTPA findings of pulmonary emboli with RV dilatation (RV/LV ratio 1.2) indicating intermediate-high risk PE requiring admission and close monitoring
Initiates immediate therapeutic anticoagulation: Rivaroxaban 15mg BD loading dose for 21 days, then 20mg daily maintenance (eTG first-line for acute PE in haemodynamically stable patient)
Immediately ceases combined oral contraceptive pill (major VTE risk factor, absolute contraindication after VTE) and counsels on alternative contraception (progesterone-only methods)
Performs appropriate risk stratification: Identifies intermediate-high risk PE (RV dysfunction, elevated troponin/BNP) requiring monitored bed and consideration of thrombolysis if deteriorates
Plans appropriate duration of anticoagulation: Minimum 3 months for provoked PE (flight + OCP), consider extension to 6 months, review at haematology clinic with thrombophilia results

Orders thrombophilia screening (appropriate in young patient age 42 with provoked VTE) but correctly defers testing until after completing anticoagulation (results affected by acute VTE and anticoagulants)
Provides patient education on bleeding precautions, signs of recurrent VTE, VTE prevention for future travel, and importance of anticoagulation compliance
Arranges appropriate follow-up: GP within 1 week, haematology at 3 months for anticoagulation duration review, contraception counselling, screening for post-PE sequelae (CTEPH)

learning_objectives: Apply Wells Score for Pulmonary Embolism to stratify pre-test probability (score 0-1 low, 2-6 moderate, >6 high) and guide investigation pathway (low Wells + negative D-dimer excludes PE, high Wells requires CTPA regardless of D-dimer)

Interpret D-dimer in context: High sensitivity but low specificity (elevated in PE, DVT, infection, malignancy, pregnancy, post-op, elderly) - cannot diagnose PE alone, requires imaging confirmation if elevated with moderate-high clinical probability
Recognize clinical features of pulmonary embolism: Pleuritic chest pain, dyspnoea, haemoptysis, tachycardia, hypoxia, clinical DVT signs (calf swelling, tenderness)

Interpret CTPA findings of PE (filling defects in pulmonary arteries) and recognize features of RV dysfunction/strain (RV/LV ratio >1.0, RV dilatation, interventricular septum flattening) indicating intermediate-high risk PE

Initiate appropriate anticoagulation for acute PE: Direct oral anticoagulant (rivaroxaban 15mg BD × 21 days, then 20mg daily) as first-line per eTG for haemodynamically stable PE with normal renal function

Identify and address VTE risk factors: Combined oral contraceptive pill (3-4× VTE risk, ABSOLUTE contraindication after VTE - never restart), long-haul flights (>4 hours), sedentary lifestyle, immobilization

Determine appropriate duration of anticoagulation: Provoked PE (clear reversible trigger like surgery, flight, OCP) = 3-6 months; Unprovoked PE or high-risk thrombophilia = consider indefinite anticoagulation

Provide VTE prevention counselling: Alternative contraception (progesterone-only methods safe), flight precautions (hydration, leg exercises, compression stockings), bleeding precautions on anticoagulation
